domain.title: Operating Systems
domain.tag: scheduling · virtual memory · I/O · the kernel boundary · containers
domain.why: Every program you'll ever write runs on top of an operating system, and when something mysteriously breaks — a program freezes, two programs fight over the same file, memory runs out — the real answer is almost always sitting in the OS layer. Most people who 'know Linux' just know the commands. This domain is about understanding what's actually happening when you run them, which is the difference that shows up the moment something goes wrong.

L0.body:
# every task the kernel knows about, threads included
ps -eLf | head
# TID != PID means it is a thread of another process
ps -o pid,tid,comm,nlwp -p 1
# the kernel's own view of one task
ls /proc/self/task/
cat /proc/self/status | grep -E 'Threads|Pid|Tgid'

concepts.L1: An address space, a file descriptor table, credentials, and one or more threads of execution. On Linux, a thread is a task sharing the address space — `clone()` with flags, not a separate concept.
concepts.L2: Linux has no separate thread abstraction in the kernel. Processes and threads are both `task_struct`; what differs is which resources were shared at clone time. That's why `ps -eLf` shows threads as tasks and why the pthread API is a userspace convention over `clone`.
concepts.L3: Read `/proc/self/status`: `Pid` is the kernel's task id, `Tgid` is the thread group id. For a single-threaded program they are equal, which is why the distinction stays invisible. Call `clone(CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_VM|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|...)` and you get a second `task_struct` with a new `Pid` and the same `Tgid`. getpid() returns the Tgid; gettid() returns the Pid. Everything userspace calls 'the process' is really 'the thread group', and every per-process resource -- mm_struct, files_struct, signal_struct -- is a refcounted object that clone either shares or copies.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program has {n} pthreads running. How many task_struct objects exist for it, how many mm_struct objects, and what does getpid() return in each thread?
L4.answer: n task_structs (one per thread), exactly one mm_struct shared by all of them, and getpid() returns the same value (the Tgid) in every thread. gettid() is what differs.
L4.explanation: Threads are tasks that shared the address space at clone time. The mm_struct is refcounted, not duplicated. POSIX demands one PID per process, so Linux exposes the thread group id as the PID and hides the per-task id behind gettid().

L4.prompt_tpl: A process has {n} threads. What does `ls /proc/self/task/ | wc -l` print from inside one of them?
L4.answer: n -- one directory per thread in the thread group, named by tid.
L4.explanation: /proc/PID/task is the thread group's membership list. It is the cheapest way to see that Linux really does model threads as tasks, with no separate thread object anywhere in the kernel.

concepts.t: clone3 and the flags that make a thread
concepts.L1: One syscall creates every kind of task. `clone3()` (and legacy `clone()`) takes a flag set naming which resources the child shares with the parent rather than copies. fork, vfork and pthread_create are three named points in that flag space.
concepts.L2: The flags are not independent: CLONE_THREAD requires CLONE_SIGHAND, which requires CLONE_VM. You cannot ask for a task that shares signal handlers but not memory. So 'a thread without a shared address space' is not expressible on Linux -- the threads-versus-processes question is really a question about flags.
concepts.L3: clone3() takes a `struct clone_args` by pointer with a size field, so new flags can be added without another syscall number -- that was the whole point of adding it in 5.3. Reading a flag set tells you exactly what you get. CLONE_VM shares the mm_struct, so a pointer means the same thing in both tasks. Without it the child gets a copy-on-write duplicate. CLONE_FILES shares the files_struct, so a `dup2` in one task is visible in the other; without it the fd numbers are copied but they point at the same open file descriptions. CLONE_THREAD puts the child in the same thread group, so it shares the PID, dies with the group on exit_group(), and never generates SIGCHLD.

L4.prompt_tpl: Task A clones a child with CLONE_FILES but NOT CLONE_VM. A then calls `close({fd})`. Is that fd still usable in the child? Now the reverse: CLONE_VM but not CLONE_FILES, and A closes the fd. Same question.
L4.answer: With CLONE_FILES the fd table is shared, so the close is visible in the child and the fd is gone there too. With only CLONE_VM the fd table was copied at clone time, so the child keeps its own descriptor referring to the same open file description; the close in A only drops A's reference.
L4.explanation: CLONE_VM and CLONE_FILES are orthogonal. Sharing memory does not share descriptors and sharing descriptors does not share memory. This is exactly the axis fork and pthread_create differ on, and knowing they are separate is the point of the flag model.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can Linux not offer 'a thread that has its own address space but shares signal handlers'?
L4.answer: Because the flag dependency runs the other way: CLONE_SIGHAND is only permitted together with CLONE_VM. Signal handler state points into the address space (handler function addresses, sigaltstack), so sharing handlers without sharing memory would let one task install a handler at an address that means nothing in the other.
L4.explanation: The dependency is enforced in copy_process(); asking for the combination returns EINVAL. It is a semantic constraint, not an implementation shortcut.

concepts.L1: `fork()` duplicates the address space lazily — pages are marked read-only and copied on first write. `exec()` then replaces it entirely.
concepts.L2: The page table itself is copied eagerly, which is why forking a process with a 100GB heap is slow even though no data pages are duplicated. This is exactly why Redis's background save can stall a large instance and why `posix_spawn` or `vfork` exist.
concepts.L3: An 8 GiB anonymous mapping with 4 KiB pages needs 2,097,152 last-level PTEs, which is 2,097,152 * 8 bytes = 16 MiB of PTE data plus the higher directory levels. fork() must walk and duplicate all of it while holding mmap_lock for write, and it must also flush the TLB because the parent's writable entries are being downgraded to read-only. None of the 8 GiB of data moves. This is why Redis BGSAVE stalls proportionally to dataset size, why `vfork()` (which shares the mm and suspends the parent) and `posix_spawn()` exist for the fork-then-exec case, and why huge pages help fork as well as the TLB: 2 MiB pages cut the PTE count by 512.

L4.prompt_tpl: A process has {g} GiB of resident anonymous memory in 4 KiB pages. Ignoring upper page-table levels, how many bytes of last-level PTEs must fork() duplicate, given 8-byte PTEs?
L4.explanation: Each 4 KiB page needs one 8-byte PTE, so PTE bytes are $1/512$ of mapped bytes. That fraction is small but the work is serial, cache-hostile pointer chasing under mmap_lock, which is why a 64 GiB fork is measurably slow while copying zero data.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {g} GiB Redis instance forks for BGSAVE and the parent stalls for tens of milliseconds. What is the dominant cost?
L4.answer: Duplicating the page tables and the TLB flush that write-protecting the parent's mappings requires.
options: Copying the heap data into the child
Duplicating the page tables and the TLB flush that write-protecting the parent's mappings requires
Serialising the RDB file to disk in the parent
L4.explanation: No heap data is copied at fork time -- that happens lazily and lands in the child's later faults. RDB serialisation happens in the child, after fork returns. The parent's stall is the page-table walk plus the TLB shootdown, both proportional to mapped size.

concepts.t: exec: what is replaced and what survives

L0.body:
# fds survive exec unless they are marked close-on-exec
bash -c 'exec 9< /etc/hostname; ls -l /proc/self/fd/9'

# see the flag itself: the 8th field of fdinfo, bit 0 = FD_CLOEXEC
cat /proc/self/fdinfo/1

# what an exec keeps: pid, ppid, cwd, umask, fds without CLOEXEC,
# pending signals, nice value, rlimits, cgroup, namespaces
# what it destroys: the address space, all threads but the caller,
# signal HANDLERS (reset to default), mmaps, and the heap
L0.cloze:
execve() replaces the {{c1::address space}} but keeps the {{c2::pid}}.
Signal dispositions that were {{c3::handled}} are reset to SIG_DFL; ignored ones stay ignored.
Open fds survive unless opened with {{c4::O_CLOEXEC}}.

concepts.L1: execve() keeps the task and throws away its contents: a new address space is built from the ELF image, all other threads in the group are killed, and the heap and mappings are gone. The pid, parent, cwd, umask, rlimits, cgroup, namespaces and non-CLOEXEC descriptors survive.
concepts.L2: Signal handlers are reset to SIG_DFL across exec but ignored signals stay ignored -- so a SIGPIPE your shell ignored is still ignored in the program it launched, and that is a real source of 'works in the terminal, hangs in cron'. Descriptors are the other half: anything without O_CLOEXEC leaks into every child you spawn.
concepts.L3: Handlers cannot survive: they are addresses in an address space that no longer exists. Dispositions can, because SIG_DFL and SIG_IGN are not addresses. That asymmetry is in POSIX and it is why a program inheriting SIG_IGN for SIGPIPE writes into a closed pipe and gets EPIPE instead of dying -- if it does not check the return value it loops forever. Descriptor leaks are the second failure mode: a server that opens a listening socket without O_CLOEXEC and later forks a helper hands the helper the socket, so restarting the server fails with EADDRINUSE until the helper dies. Always pass O_CLOEXEC at open time; a later fcntl races with a fork in another thread.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service opens its listening socket, then later runs a helper via fork+exec. After a restart it fails with EADDRINUSE for {s} seconds even though the service process is gone. What is wrong and what is the one-word fix?
L4.answer: The listening socket was opened without O_CLOEXEC, so the exec'd helper inherited it and still holds the port open. Fix: O_CLOEXEC (or SOCK_CLOEXEC on socket()).
L4.explanation: SO_REUSEADDR does not help: the port is genuinely still bound by a live process. `ls -l /proc/PID/fd` on the helper shows the inherited socket. This is why modern APIs default to close-on-exec in every language wrapper written after about 2010.

L4.prompt_tpl: A shell script does `trap '' SIGPIPE` and then runs a program that writes {n} MB into a pipe whose reader exits early. The program has no SIGPIPE handler of its own. What happens, and why is it different from running the program directly?
L4.answer: SIG_IGN survives exec, so the program inherits an ignored SIGPIPE: instead of being killed it gets EPIPE from write(). Run directly, the default disposition applies and the process dies silently at the first write. Same program, opposite outcome, decided by the parent.
L4.explanation: Handlers are reset at exec because they are addresses; SIG_IGN is not an address, so it is inherited. A program that ignores write() errors turns this into an infinite loop, which is the classic 'hangs only under the supervisor' bug.

L0.body:
# a zombie is an exited child nobody has reaped: State Z
ps -eo pid,ppid,state,comm --sort=state | grep -w Z

# reap without blocking, in a loop, because SIGCHLD does not queue
#   while (waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) > 0) ;

# claim orphaned descendants instead of losing them to pid 1
prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, 1, 0, 0, 0);

# who is my reaper?
grep NSpid /proc/self/status
L0.cloze:
A zombie holds only the {{c1::exit status}} and its pid, no memory.
It is removed when the parent calls {{c2::wait}} (or waitpid/waitid).
An orphan is re-parented to the nearest {{c3::subreaper}}, or to pid 1 if there is none.

concepts.L1: An exited child stays in the task table as a zombie until its parent collects the status with wait/waitpid/waitid. If the parent dies first the child is re-parented to the nearest ancestor marked PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, or failing that to pid 1.
concepts.L2: SIGCHLD is a standard signal, so it does not queue: three children exiting close together can deliver one signal. A handler that calls waitpid once per signal leaks zombies forever. The handler must loop on waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) until it returns 0 or -1.
concepts.L3: A zombie occupies no memory and no fds -- the address space was torn down at exit. It holds a pid and an exit status, and pids are finite (`/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max`). Leak enough and fork() returns EAGAIN machine-wide. The queueing rule is the trap: standard signals are a bit in a pending mask, so N deliveries while blocked collapse to one; the correct handler is a WNOHANG loop. Containers compound it -- pid 1 there is usually the application, not init, so if it never reaps, orphans pile up in that pid namespace. That is what `--init` and PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER exist to fix.

L4.prompt_tpl: A daemon installs a SIGCHLD handler that calls `waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG)` exactly once, then spawns {n} short-lived children in a burst. Zombies accumulate. Explain precisely why and give the fix.
L4.answer: SIGCHLD is a standard (non-realtime) signal, so pending instances coalesce into a single bit: several children exiting during one handler run deliver one SIGCHLD, and one waitpid call reaps one child. Fix: loop `while (waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) > 0) ;` inside the handler.
L4.explanation: Signal counts are not a reliable event count for any standard signal. The loop-until-drained pattern here is the same discipline as draining an edge-triggered epoll fd until EAGAIN: the notification says 'something changed', not 'exactly one thing changed'.

L4.prompt_tpl: A container runs a shell as pid 1 which starts a server that itself forks workers. Workers that outlive their immediate parent become zombies and never disappear. Why does running the container with an init process fix it?
L4.answer: Orphans are re-parented to pid 1 of their pid namespace. In the container that is the shell, which never calls wait, so the zombies stay. A real init (or a subreaper) loops on wait() and reaps whatever it inherits, so orphaned tasks are collected.
L4.explanation: Outside a container this is invisible because the host pid 1 (systemd) always reaps. Pid namespaces give the container its own pid 1 and thereby its own reaping obligation -- which is what docker --init and tini supply.

# voluntary vs involuntary switches for one process
pidstat -w -p <pid> 1
# system-wide: cs column
vmstat 1
# per-task totals
grep ctxt /proc/<pid>/status
# what it actually costs: measure, do not guess
perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations,dTLB-load-misses,\
cache-misses -p <pid> -- sleep 10
# off-CPU time, which is the part that matters
# bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { @[comm] = count(); }'
L0.cloze:
pidstat -w distinguishes {{c1::voluntary}} switches (the task blocked) from
{{c2::involuntary}} ones (the task was preempted).
The counter that shows the *indirect* cost is not a switch count at all -- it is {{c3::dTLB-load-misses}} and cache-misses.

concepts.L1: Roughly 1–5μs directly, but the real cost is the cold cache and TLB afterward — often 10–50μs of degraded performance before locality is re-established.
concepts.L2: The indirect cost dominates and doesn't appear in any context-switch counter. This is the argument for thread pinning, for reducing thread counts below core counts, and for why oversubscribed thread pools underperform in ways that look inexplicable in a profile.
concepts.L3: The direct cost is register save, page-table pointer swap (CR3 on x86-64), and scheduler bookkeeping: roughly one to a few microseconds. What follows is the real bill. The new task finds L1/L2 filled with the previous task's lines and the TLB either flushed or, with PCID, merely cold for its own entries. Every early access misses. For a 4 MiB working set the refill is tens of thousands of misses at roughly 80 ns each, and that cost is billed to the *new* task's instructions -- a profile shows 'this loop got slower' with no switch in sight. Hence: pin threads, keep pools at or below core count, and read cs alongside cache counters.

L4.prompt_tpl: A thread's working set is {w} MiB of 64-byte lines, all evicted by a context switch. At {ns} ns per LLC miss and perfect overlap of 4 outstanding misses, roughly how many microseconds does the refill add? Answer with the added time in microseconds.
L4.answer: lines = w * 2^{20} / 64; time = lines * ns / 4 nanoseconds. For w=4, ns=80: 65536 lines * 80 / 4 = 1310720 ns = about 1310 microseconds of extra memory latency spread over the refill.
L4.explanation: The number is deliberately crude -- prefetchers and reuse cut it a lot -- but the order of magnitude is the point: the indirect cost can dwarf the 1-5 microsecond switch itself, and it appears in cache counters, never in the cs column.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service with {t} worker threads on a {c}-core box shows high `cs` in vmstat and a flat CPU profile with no obvious hot function. What single configuration change do you try first and what counter confirms it worked?
L4.answer: Reduce the pool to roughly the core count (or pin threads with taskset/sched_setaffinity). Confirm with perf stat: context-switches and cpu-migrations fall, and dTLB-load-misses plus LLC-load-misses fall with them while throughput rises.
L4.explanation: Oversubscription costs you locality, not CPU time, so it is invisible in utilisation and in any on-CPU profile. The confirming evidence has to be cache and TLB counters, because those are where the loss actually shows up.

concepts.L1: CFS used a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime, targeting fairness. Since kernel 6.6, EEVDF (Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First) replaced it, adding explicit latency targets per task.
concepts.L2: Most material online still describes CFS as current. Knowing EEVDF replaced it — and that it exists to give latency-sensitive tasks a deadline rather than just a fairness share — is a genuinely current detail that dates your knowledge correctly.
concepts.L3: CFS answered one question -- who is furthest behind on virtual runtime -- and handled latency only indirectly, via sched_min_granularity and interactivity heuristics. EEVDF answers two: eligibility (is this task's lag non-negative) and urgency (which eligible task has the earliest virtual deadline). A task's deadline comes from its requested slice, so a shorter request buys lower latency at the same share rather than more CPU; `sched_setattr()` carries it as `sched_runtime`. Mainline is now 7.x and the longterm branches are 6.18, 6.12 and 6.6 -- on anything supported you are on EEVDF, and material calling CFS current is describing pre-6.6 kernels.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two CPU-bound tasks share one core with equal weight. Task A asks for a {a} ms slice, task B for the default. Over {s} seconds, what happens?
L4.answer: Both get about 50 percent of the CPU; A is scheduled more often in shorter bursts, so its worst-case wakeup latency is lower.
options: A gets proportionally more CPU because it is scheduled more often
Both get about 50 percent of the CPU; A is scheduled more often in shorter bursts, so its worst-case wakeup latency is lower
A is treated as a real-time task and preempts B whenever it is runnable
L4.explanation: Under EEVDF the request size sets the virtual deadline, not the share. Share comes from weight (nice / cpu.weight). Decoupling latency from share is the entire reason EEVDF replaced CFS -- previously the only way to ask for lower latency was to ask for more CPU.

L4.prompt_tpl: You read a blog post dated {y} that says 'Linux uses CFS, which keeps tasks in a red-black tree ordered by vruntime'. State what is now wrong, what is still right, and how you would check on the machine in front of you.
L4.answer: Still right: the fair class is weight-proportional and virtual time is the accounting unit. Now wrong: since 6.6 the picking rule is EEVDF -- select among tasks with non-negative lag the one with the earliest virtual deadline -- not simply leftmost vruntime. Check with `uname -r` and `cat /proc/<pid>/sched`, which reports deadline and lag fields on EEVDF kernels.
L4.explanation: The distinction matters because it changes the advice: on EEVDF a latency-sensitive task should request a smaller slice rather than a lower nice value. Knowing which kernel you are on before quoting scheduler behaviour is the actual skill.

concepts.t: EEVDF: lag, eligibility and the virtual deadline

L0.cloze:
lag = (fair share so far) - (service received). A task is {{c1::eligible}} when its lag is non-negative.
Among eligible tasks EEVDF runs the earliest {{c2::virtual deadline}}.
virtual deadline = virtual eligible time + (requested slice / {{c3::weight}}).

concepts.L1: EEVDF splits scheduling into two questions. Lag measures how much service a task is owed relative to its weight; a task is eligible only when its lag is at least zero. Among eligible tasks it runs the one whose virtual deadline -- eligible time plus its request scaled by weight -- is earliest.
concepts.L2: People read 'deadline' and think SCHED_DEADLINE, a real-time policy with admission control and hard guarantees. EEVDF's virtual deadline is an ordering key inside the fair class, not a promise. Missing it costs you nothing; it only decides who goes next.
concepts.L3: Under CFS the only latency knob was nice, and lowering nice raised your share as a side effect: you could not say 'wake me promptly but give me no more CPU'. EEVDF separates them. Weight sets the share, since lag is measured against weight-proportional entitlement. The requested slice sets the deadline: a smaller request means an earlier deadline, so the task is picked sooner and runs less -- more switches, same total service. Lag also replaces the CFS wakeup hack: a task that slept returns with positive lag, so it is immediately eligible and preempts naturally rather than via a vruntime bonus. Negative lag after a long run makes a task ineligible until virtual time catches up.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two tasks share a core. Task A has weight {wa}, task B weight {wb}, and both request the same slice. Derive each task's steady-state CPU share, and state what changes if A halves its requested slice.
L4.answer: Share is weight-proportional: A gets wa/(wa+wb), B gets wb/(wa+wb). For wa=1024, wb=1024 that is 50/50; for wa=2048, wb=512 it is 80/20. Halving A's requested slice does not change the share at all -- it halves A's virtual deadline horizon, so A is picked about twice as often for half as long. Latency improves, share does not.
L4.explanation: This is the whole design: lag and eligibility are computed from weight, the deadline from the request. Conflating the two is the most common error when people first read the EEVDF documentation.

L4.prompt_tpl: An audio thread needs to wake every {p} ms and run for well under a millisecond. Someone proposes SCHED_FIFO priority 50. Give one reason that is risky and what the EEVDF-era alternative is.
L4.answer: SCHED_FIFO preempts every normal task and never yields until it blocks, so a bug that spins livelocks the CPU (mitigated only by sched_rt_runtime_us). The EEVDF-era alternative is to stay in SCHED_NORMAL and request a small slice via sched_setattr's sched_runtime, which lowers wakeup latency without granting the ability to starve everything else.
L4.explanation: Real-time classes are a sledgehammer: correct when you genuinely need bounded latency and you control the code, dangerous when what you actually wanted was 'schedule me promptly'. The slice request expresses the latter directly.

In pthreads that is {{c3::PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT}}; in the kernel, FUTEX_LOCK_PI.

A plain futex word is just a value, so FUTEX_WAIT can boost nobody; FUTEX_LOCK_PI stores the owner tid in the word, letting the kernel raise the owner to the waiter's priority and drop it at unlock. L4.explanation: The timeout is why the exemption exists -- an automatic restart would reset the full 1000 ms each time, so a signal every 900 ms would make the call never time out. POSIX pushes the decision to the caller precisely so the deadline can be recomputed correctly.

concepts.L1: Four or five level page tables on x86-64, walked by hardware on a TLB miss. Each level is a memory access, so a full walk is four dependent loads.
concepts.L2: A TLB miss costs four memory accesses that themselves may miss cache. For large working sets this can exceed the cost of the data access itself, and it appears in no cache-miss counter — you need `dTLB-load-misses` specifically.
concepts.L3: Each level indexes 9 bits of the virtual address into a 512-entry table, giving 48 bits of address space over 4 levels (9*4 + 12 offset). The walk is serial: you cannot fetch level N+1 until level N returns, so the four accesses do not overlap. They are cached -- page-table lines live in the normal data caches, and there are dedicated paging-structure caches -- but for a working set that thrashes the TLB, the walk lines get evicted too. Then a single data access costs up to five memory accesses. A 1536-entry L2 TLB with 4 KiB pages covers only 6 MiB, so any larger random-access working set spends most of its time translating rather than loading. This is what huge pages fix.

L4.prompt_tpl: A CPU has a {n}-entry second-level dTLB. What is its reach with 4 KiB pages, and with 2 MiB pages, in MiB and GiB respectively? Answer with the 4 KiB-page reach in MiB.
L4.answer: reach_4k = n * 4 KiB; reach_2M = n * 2 MiB. For n=1536: 6 MiB and 3 GiB. For n=2048: 8 MiB and 4 GiB. For n=3072: 12 MiB and 6 GiB.
L4.explanation: TLB reach, not TLB entry count, is the number that matters. Switching to 2 MiB pages multiplies reach by 512 with no change to the entry count, which is why huge pages help pointer-chasing workloads whose data comfortably fits in DRAM but not in TLB reach.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive why x86-64 4-level paging gives {b} bits of usable virtual address, from the 9-bits-per-level, 4 KiB-page structure.

Four levels index 4 * 9 = 36 bits, and the page offset within a 4 KiB page is 12 bits, so 36 + 12 = 48 bits. Bits 48-63 must be a sign extension of bit 47, which is the canonical-address rule. Five-level paging (la57) adds a level for 57 bits.
L4.explanation: The 9-bit fan-out is not arbitrary: it falls out of making each page table exactly one page. That single constraint determines the level count, the address width, and why the fifth level was the natural way to extend it.

#  6 D      dirty    -- set by hardware on write, drives writeback

Hardware sets {{c3::accessed}} and {{c4::dirty}}; software clears them -- that is how page reclaim ages pages.

concepts.L1: A page table entry is one machine word holding a physical frame number plus permission and status bits. Hardware reads it on every TLB miss and writes back the accessed and dirty bits; the kernel owns everything else.
concepts.L2: When the present bit is clear the hardware ignores the rest of the entry entirely, so the kernel repurposes those bits -- for a swap slot, a migration entry, or a NUMA hinting marker. A 'not present' page is therefore not necessarily absent; the fault handler reads the same word to find out what it actually is.
concepts.L3: This dual use is the mechanism behind most of virtual memory. Copy-on-write clears R/W but leaves P set: the fault is a protection fault, and the handler copies the page and restores write permission. Demand paging clears P entirely with the rest zero: the handler allocates a zero page. Swap clears P and stores a swap type plus offset in the remaining bits: the handler reads the block back. Automatic NUMA balancing clears P and marks it PROT_NONE so the next touch traps and reveals which node the thread is on. Every one of these is 'a fault happened' at the hardware level and something entirely different in the handler, which is why /proc/vmstat distinguishes so many fault counters.

options: The CPU reads the frame number anyway and faults only on a permission mismatch
The CPU raises a page fault and ignores the other bits entirely; the kernel handler interprets them
The access succeeds but the accessed bit is not updated
L4.explanation: Present=0 means the entry has no architectural meaning beyond 'fault'. That is precisely what lets the kernel store swap slots, migration entries and NUMA markers there. The handler, not the hardware, decides what kind of fault it was.

L4.prompt_tpl: How does the kernel use the accessed bit to decide which pages to reclaim, and why does it need to clear it?

Clearing is what turns a sticky flag into a sampling window, which is what makes the two-list LRU approximation work.
L4.explanation: Without clearing, every page that was ever touched looks equally hot forever. The clear-and-recheck cycle costs a TLB flush for the affected entries, which is why reclaim is not free even when it evicts nothing.

An eBPF program is proven safe before load -- bounded, memory-checked, terminating, restricted to a fixed helper surface -- and it aggregates in kernel space so only summaries cross to userspace. The residual cost is per-event instructions in the tens of nanoseconds, not a stop like ptrace.
L4.explanation: The safety argument is what changed production debugging practice. It is also why the verifier's strictness is a feature rather than an obstacle: every rejection is a proof obligation you failed to discharge.

L4.prompt_tpl: A program reads `data[idx]` from a {n}-byte map value after checking `if (idx > {n})`. The verifier rejects it with an out-of-bounds error. What is wrong?
L4.answer: The check is off by one: idx == n passes but is out of bounds for a zero-indexed buffer of n bytes. The verifier tracks the register's proven range as [0, n] after the check and correctly concludes the access can exceed the map value. The fix is `if (idx >= n) return 0;` so the tracked range becomes [0, n-1].
L4.explanation: The verifier reports what it proved, not what you intended, and its complaint here is literally correct. Reading the range it printed for the register in the log is usually faster than re-reading the source.

L4.answer: A mean collapses the distribution, and I/O latency is rarely unimodal. A histogram with one cluster near 0.1 ms and another near 20 ms says most requests are served from a fast path -- device cache, or a cached mapping -- while a minority take a slow path, perhaps a different device, a queue, or garbage collection inside the SSD. The mean describes neither population and predicts no percentile.
L4.explanation: Whenever a latency mean and a p99 disagree by an order of magnitude, the distribution is multimodal and the mean is actively misleading. eBPF histograms are cheap because bucketing happens in kernel space, so there is no reason to settle for an average.

concepts.t: bpftrace: probes and the one-liners worth owning

L0.body:
# what can I attach to?
sudo bpftrace -l 'tracepoint:syscalls:*' | head
sudo bpftrace -l 'kprobe:vfs_*'

# 1. who is exec'ing what
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_execve
  { printf("%s %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }'

# 2. latency histogram of one syscall
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_read { @t[tid] = nsecs; }
  tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_read /@t[tid]/
  { @us = hist((nsecs - @t[tid]) / 1000); delete(@t[tid]); }'

# 3. kernel stacks for a rare event
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:oom_kill_process { printf("%s\n", kstack); }'
L0.cloze:
Probe types: {{c1::tracepoint}} (stable ABI, preferred), kprobe (any kernel function, unstable), uprobe, and profile/interval.
The map idiom is store {{c2::nsecs}} keyed by tid on entry, subtract on exit, and aggregate with hist().
{{c3::-l}} lists available probes, with globs.

concepts.L1: bpftrace is an awk-like language over eBPF: a list of probes, optional filters, and actions that write into aggregating maps. It exists for the questions no packaged tool answers, and it compiles a program per invocation.
concepts.L2: Prefer tracepoints to kprobes. A tracepoint is a stable interface the kernel promises to keep; a kprobe attaches to an arbitrary function whose name, arguments and even existence change between releases, so a kprobe one-liner that works today can silently attach to nothing after an upgrade -- or fail to load at all.
concepts.L3: The entry-exit timing idiom is the one to internalise, because most latency questions have that shape: timestamp into a map keyed by tid at entry, subtract at exit, aggregate into a histogram, delete the key. Deleting matters -- a map accumulating one entry per tid on a thread-churning host hits its size limit and silently drops data. Filters run in the kernel, so `/pid == 1234/` costs almost nothing and beats printing everything and grepping. Output is intentionally aggregate: printf per event on a high-frequency probe floods the ring buffer, so hist(), count() and sum() are the normal actions.

L4.prompt_tpl: Write the structure of a bpftrace program measuring the latency distribution of a {f} call for one pid, and say which probe type you use and why.
L4.answer: Use the syscalls tracepoints, not kprobes, because they are a stable interface. Structure: `tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_X /pid == P/ { @t[tid] = nsecs; }` then `tracepoint:syscalls:sys_exit_X /@t[tid]/ { @us = hist((nsecs - @t[tid]) / 1000); delete(@t[tid]); }`. The pid filter runs in the kernel, the histogram aggregates in the kernel, and the delete keeps the map bounded.
L4.explanation: Three properties make this production-safe: in-kernel filtering, in-kernel aggregation, and a bounded map. Dropping any one of them turns a negligible-overhead probe into a source of load or of silently lost data.

L4.prompt_tpl: A one-liner does `tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_write {{ printf("%d %s\n", pid, comm); }}` on a host doing {n} writes per second. What goes wrong?
L4.answer: One printf per event at that rate overwhelms the perf output buffer: bpftrace reports lost events, the terminal cannot keep up, and the CPU cost of formatting and copying every record becomes significant. Replace it with an aggregation -- `@[comm] = count();` -- which keeps everything in a kernel map and copies only the summary when the program exits, and add a pid or comm filter if you only care about one process.
L4.explanation: eBPF's low overhead comes from aggregating in kernel space. Per-event output re-imposes exactly the cost the design avoids, which is why every bcc tool built for high-frequency probes emits histograms or counts rather than lines.

cd /sys/kernel/tracing         # legacy path: /sys/kernel/debug/tracing

cat available_tracers          # function function_graph blk nop ...
echo function_graph > current_tracer
echo vfs_read > set_ftrace_filter

tracefs is mounted at {{c1::/sys/kernel/tracing}} on modern kernels.
Select a tracer by writing to {{c2::current_tracer}}; {{c3::function_graph}} records entry, exit and duration per function.
Restrict the cost with {{c4::set_ftrace_filter}} -- tracing every kernel function is not viable on a busy machine.

concepts.L1: ftrace is the kernel's built-in tracer, driven entirely by files under tracefs. It offers function and function_graph tracers, the full tracepoint event set, and per-CPU ring buffers, with no userspace tooling required.
concepts.L2: The function tracer instruments every kernel function, so enabling it unfiltered on a busy machine can slow the system to the point of unusability. set_ftrace_filter is not an optimisation, it is a prerequisite -- and remember to write nop back to current_tracer, because ftrace stays on after your shell exits.
concepts.L3: ftrace's value is that it is always there: no compiler, no bcc, no headers, nothing to install, which matters on a locked-down host. function_graph is its distinctive capability, printing a call tree with a duration per function, so you can see that vfs_read spent its time in the filesystem rather than the block layer without writing a program. eBPF wins on programmability and aggregation: ftrace hands you text to post-process, eBPF summarises in the kernel. The practical division is that ftrace answers 'what did the kernel do, in order' and eBPF answers 'how much, aggregated by what'. Both read from the same tracepoints underneath.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a locked-down host with no compiler, no bcc and no bpftrace, you must find out where a {ms} ms vfs_read is spending its time. Give the ftrace sequence and the one mistake that would take the machine down.
L4.answer: cd /sys/kernel/tracing; echo function_graph > current_tracer; echo vfs_read > set_ftrace_filter; echo 1 > tracing_on; reproduce; echo 0 > tracing_on; cat trace; echo nop > current_tracer. The fatal mistake is enabling function or function_graph without writing set_ftrace_filter first: tracing every kernel function on a busy host can slow it to a standstill.
L4.explanation: function_graph with a filter shows the call tree beneath vfs_read with per-function durations, which localises the time to the filesystem, the block layer, or a lock. Resetting current_tracer to nop matters because ftrace state is global and outlives your shell.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have both ftrace and eBPF available on the same host. Give one question where ftrace is the better tool and one where eBPF is, for a workload doing {n} operations per second.
L4.answer: ftrace: 'what exactly did the kernel do during this one slow operation, in order' -- function_graph gives an ordered call tree with durations that no aggregation can reconstruct. eBPF: 'what is the latency distribution of this operation across all n per second, broken down by process' -- in-kernel histograms handle that volume, whereas ftrace would produce an unmanageable text stream.
L4.explanation: The split is sequence versus statistics. It also maps onto cost: ftrace's per-event text output does not scale with rate, while eBPF's aggregation does but discards ordering unless you deliberately record it.

concepts.t: Core dumps: producing and reading one

L0.body:
# 1. allow dumps at all
ulimit -c unlimited
cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern     # a leading | pipes to a program

# systemd hosts pipe to systemd-coredump:
coredumpctl list
coredumpctl info <pid>
coredumpctl debug <pid>               # opens gdb on the dump

# plain file pattern: %p pid, %e comm, %t time, %s signal
sysctl -w kernel.core_pattern='/var/cores/core.%e.%p.%t'

# 2. read it
gdb /path/to/binary /var/cores/core.myprog.1234.1735689600
#   (gdb) bt full
#   (gdb) thread apply all bt
#   (gdb) info registers
L0.cloze:
A dump is only written if {{c1::RLIMIT_CORE}} is non-zero -- `ulimit -c unlimited`.
If /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern begins with {{c2::|}}, the dump is piped to that program instead of written to a file.
The first two commands in gdb are `bt full` and `thread apply all {{c3::bt}}`.

concepts.L1: A core dump is a snapshot of the process's memory and register state at the moment a fatal signal was delivered. It is written according to core_pattern, subject to RLIMIT_CORE, and read with gdb against the same binary and its debug symbols.
concepts.L2: The three reasons you get no dump: RLIMIT_CORE is zero (the default in many shells and container runtimes), core_pattern pipes to a handler absent from the container's mount namespace, or the binary is stripped so the dump exists but every frame is an address.
concepts.L3: In containers this is genuinely awkward. core_pattern is a host-wide setting -- there is no per-namespace version -- so a container cannot choose its own, and a piped handler is executed in the host's namespaces while the crashing process's paths are in the container's. The workable setups are a host-side systemd-coredump collecting everything, or a plain file pattern writing to a bind-mounted path. Dumps are also enormous: coredump_filter includes anonymous and shared mappings by default, so a 40 GiB heap gives a 40 GiB core -- tune /proc/PID/coredump_filter if you only need stacks. For a hung rather than crashed process, `gcore <pid>` dumps without killing it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A containerised service segfaults roughly {n} times a day and no core file ever appears in the configured directory. Give three independent causes and how to test each.
L4.answer: (1) RLIMIT_CORE is 0 -- check `cat /proc/PID/limits` inside the container and set ulimit -c unlimited in the entrypoint. (2) core_pattern is a host setting piping to systemd-coredump, so nothing lands in the container's path -- check `cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` on the host and look at `coredumpctl list` there. (3) The target directory does not exist or is not writable in the container's mount namespace -- the kernel silently gives up, so verify the path from inside.
L4.explanation: All three fail silently, which is why 'no core file' is such a common dead end. Testing is cheap: `kill -SEGV` a sleep inside the container and see where, if anywhere, the dump appears.

L4.prompt_tpl: A process with a {g} GiB heap must be dumped for analysis, but writing {g} GiB is not acceptable. What do you change, and what do you lose?
L4.answer: Write a restrictive mask to /proc/PID/coredump_filter so file-backed private, shared and huge-page mappings are excluded and only anonymous private memory (or even just the stacks) is dumped. You lose the ability to inspect the excluded regions -- mapped files and shared segments will be absent -- so a bug whose evidence is in the heap data itself may become undiagnosable. Register state, stacks and backtraces survive.
L4.explanation: The trade is dump size against how much of the heap you can inspect. For a crash whose cause is a bad pointer or a control-flow error, stacks and registers are enough; for data corruption you need the heap and must accept the size.

concepts.L1: `vmstat`, `iostat -x`, `mpstat -P ALL`, `pidstat`, `ss -s`, `sar` for history, `perf top`, `dmesg -T`.
concepts.L2: `dmesg` first, always. OOM kills, filesystem errors, network device resets and hardware failures all land there, and a surprising number of multi-hour investigations end with a line that was in dmesg the whole time.
concepts.L3: The ordering is a method, not a list. dmesg first because it is the only source that reports events you have already missed -- an OOM kill at 03:00, a device reset, an EXT4-fs error, a NIC hang -- and a surprising share of long investigations end at a line that was sitting there the whole time. sar second when the incident is over, because everything else shows only the present. mpstat rather than a global average, because one saturated core -- a single-threaded bottleneck, or an interrupt pinned to CPU 0 -- vanishes in an average across 64 CPUs. pidstat to attribute that to a process, then PSI to decide whether any of it is real saturation. Gregg's 60-second checklist is this same sequence.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service died {h} hours ago and restarted. You have shell access now. What do you run first?
L4.answer: dmesg -T (or journalctl -k) and sar -A for the relevant interval -- the only sources that describe a window that has already passed.
options: perf top, to see what the service is doing now
dmesg -T (or journalctl -k) and sar -A for the relevant interval -- the only sources that describe a window that has already passed
iostat -x 1 and vmstat 1, to establish a live baseline
L4.explanation: Live tools describe the present, and the present is a freshly restarted process. dmesg carries kernel events with timestamps -- OOM kill, device error, filesystem error -- and sar carries recorded resource history. Everything else is for after you know roughly what happened.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {c}-core host shows {u} percent average CPU and users report slowness. Which tool from the list separates the two likely explanations, and what are they?
L4.answer: mpstat -P ALL 1. Either one CPU is at 100 percent while the rest idle -- a single-threaded bottleneck or an interrupt pinned to one core, which an average across c cores hides completely -- or all cores are genuinely lightly loaded and the delay is off-CPU, in which case check /proc/pressure and run offcputime. The per-CPU breakdown distinguishes them in one screen.
L4.explanation: Averaging over many cores is one of the most reliable ways to hide a bottleneck: at 64 cores, one fully saturated CPU adds only 1.6 percent to the mean. Per-CPU views and per-queue views exist for exactly this reason.
